title: Turning America’s Trusted Institutions Into Points of Care and Opportunity
summary: We are living in an age of extremes. On one hand, revolutionary new technology promises to deliver life-changing outcomes. On the other, we face an unprecedented shortfall in reliable care.
body_markdown:
** **


We are living in an age of extremes. On one hand, revolutionary new technology promises to deliver life-changing outcomes. On the other, we face an unprecedented shortfall in reliable care.


*Thousands of trusted institutions like libraries and schools can become points of care and opportunity. They just need one thing: access infrastructure.*


Distance still decides too much in rural America. More than 92 million Americans live in primary care shortage areas, while 137 million live in mental health shortage areas. In mental health shortage areas, just 27% of the need for care is being met.


Broadband gave communities a way to overcome geography by bringing services to people where they live instead of forcing people to travel for access. AI can push the shift much further, helping clinicians, educators, advisors, and other experts reach more people without requiring every service to exist locally.


But being connected is not the same as being able to use what technology can now deliver.


Access infrastructure closes the gap between powerful digital services and the people who need them.


**Connectivity is only the beginning**


America has spent years investing billions in broadband infrastructure, including through programs like BEAD. That investment matters enormously. Without connectivity, none of what comes next is possible.


AI now raises the stakes. A clinician can reach more patients. AI can help people navigate care, find the right provider, translate a conversation, or access expertise unavailable locally. Similar advances are emerging across education, workforce training, benefits, and other essential services.


But more capable services do not automatically create greater access.


Consider mental healthcare. Remote therapy can connect someone with a provider hundreds of miles away, while AI can support navigation, triage, translation, documentation, and other parts of the care experience. Home, however, is not always a place where someone can speak freely.


A phone and broadband connection do not help much if your kids are in the next room, your partner can hear through the wall, or you are worried someone might walk in. The same problem applies to a medical appointment, job interview, benefits conversation, tutoring session, or other high-stakes interaction.


Access requires more than a network connection. People need privacy, high-quality interaction, accessibility, and a simple way to reach the right service.


That is what we mean by access infrastructure.


## **Trusted institutions can become the missing middle**


Rural health facilities, libraries, schools, community colleges, tribal institutions, and other local organizations already form a trusted physical network across America. Many also have strong broadband and already serve as local access points for information, education, and support.


AI and remote services make the network far more valuable. A rural clinic can connect patients to specialists elsewhere. A school can connect students to training unavailable locally. A library can expand access to care, education, benefits, and other services without becoming the provider itself.


The need is growing. The Association of American Medical Colleges projects a shortage of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036, while roughly one in five physicians is already 65 or older. Communities cannot solve every shortage by recruiting more local professionals.


Technology can extend scarce expertise. Trusted institutions can give people a reliable place to reach it.


[The Rural Health Transformation Program](https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/rural-health)


gives states $50 billion over five years to expand rural healthcare, modernize technology, strengthen the workforce, and bring services closer to the people who need them. Trusted institutions can help extend the reach of those investments far beyond traditional healthcare facilities.


## **Access infrastructure has to clear four bars**


There is a big difference between putting a tablet in a booth and creating infrastructure people can rely on for an important appointment. I believe access infrastructure programs have to clear four bars.


1.


**It has to be lifelike.** When a clinician is looking for subtle visual cues or someone is interviewing for a job, video and audio quality matter. The goal should be to get as close as possible to feeling like two people are sitting in the same room.


2.


**It has to be private.** Someone talking with a doctor or counselor should not be wondering who can hear them. Privacy also has to carry through the technology so sensitive information goes where it belongs.


3.


**It has to be simple.** A person should be able to walk in and get where they need to go without becoming an expert in video conferencing software, telehealth platforms, or AI tools. The technology should help someone navigate complexity, not create more of it. Just as important, the host institution should not suddenly become responsible for running an IT help desk.


4.


**It has to be inclusive.** Age, disability, language, or digital skill should not determine whether someone can use it. If public money is paying for the infrastructure, it should work for as much of the public as possible.


The best access infrastructure makes complexity disappear. Someone should be able to walk in, get the care or service they need, and walk out without ever thinking about the technology making it possible.


AI should meet the same standard: better services, reaching more people, when and where they need them.


## **Oklahoma put the model into practice**


Oklahoma took the idea and applied it to infrastructure the state already had.


After years of investing in broadband deployment, the Oklahoma Broadband Office turned its attention to libraries, CareerTech centers, and community colleges. Instead of building an entirely new network of facilities, it asked how existing institutions could give communities access to more care and opportunity.


Through its Community Access Portals program, Oklahoma is deploying up to 175 private, connected Portals across the state.


The model is powerful because the physical infrastructure can remain useful as the services running through it evolve. A library, career tech center, rural health facility, school, or other trusted institution does not have to become something it is not. It gains a new way to connect people with services and expertise unavailable locally.


## **Put more services within reach**


RHTP gives states a rare opportunity to rethink rural access. Start with the institutions communities already trust, identify where people travel for care and other essential services, and use technology to bring more of those services closer to home.


BEAD II guidance is expected soon. While none of us have a crystal ball, it’s reasonable to expect some support for turning trusted institutions into points of care and opportunity.


AI can extend scarce expertise farther than ever before, but access infrastructure will determine who can actually reach it.
